messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (mean output in window 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (maximum voltage ever).
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple in window 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (time to reach 1.8V from 0V).
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$ (mostly), $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage: $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ for S1.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong exc, light load), S4 (weak exc), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/Cp+20%).

    *   Reference design: Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR).
    *   S2 (Heavy load): Fails $V_{out,min}$ (1.76V) and $t_{up}$.
    *   S3 (Strong exc, light load): Fails $V_{out,max}$ (5.72V), $V_{pp}$, and $dv$.
    *   S4 (Weak exc): Fails $V_{out,min}$ (1.51V), $t_{up}$, and $dv$.
    *   S5 (Low freq): Fails $dv$.
    *   Observation: The FBR lacks voltage regulation (too high in S3) and insufficient efficiency/boosting (too low in S2, S4).

    *   *Passive Rectification (FBR):* Simple, but no regulation. $V_{out}$ depends on the balance of harvested power and load.
    *   *Synchronous Switching Harvesting (SSHI):* Uses switches to invert $C_p$ voltage, significantly increasing power extraction (especially at low frequencies or high $C_p$).
    *   *Zener Clamping:* To prevent $V_{out} > 3.6\text{ V}$. Since $V_{max\_limit} = 3.6\text{ V}$, a 3.3V Zener (DZ33) is appropriate.
    *   *Voltage Regulation:* A Zener clamp is the simplest way to limit the peak.
    *   *Boosting/Efficiency:* To solve S2 and S4, we need more power. SSHI (Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor) can help.

    *   **Design 1: FBR + Zener Clamp (Standard Rectification with Overvoltage Protection)**
        *   Topology: Full bridge + $C_{out}$ + DZ33 (cathode on `out`).
        *   Rationale: Fixes S3 $V_{max}$ failure. Might still struggle with S2/S4 $V_{min}$ because it's still just an FBR.

    *   **Design 2: Parallel-SSHI (Synchronous Switching Harvesting on Inductor)**
        *   Topology: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductor $L$ $\rightarrow$ Switch $S$ $\rightarrow$ Piezo (inverted). Rectifier follows.
        *   Wait, the prompt allows SYNC and switches. The standard SSHI-L circuit:
            Piezo (pzp, pzn) connected to a switch $S$ and an inductor $L$ in parallel.
            $S$ closes at the peaks of $V_{piezo}$ to flip the charge.
            Actually, a common SSHI implementation:
            Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
            To increase energy, use an inductor $L$ and switch $S$ to flip $V_{Cp}$ relative to the rectifier input.
            Simplified SSHI: Inductor $L$ connected between pzp and a node n1, switch S between n1 and pzn.
            Actually, the most robust way to implement a boost is an SSHI-like structure or a simple buck-boost, but we only have SYNC controllers and basic components.
            Let's try a **Synchronous Charge Extraction (SCE)** or a simplified SSHI.
            S-SSHI:
            1. Piezo nodes (pzp, pzn).
            2. Rectifier from (pzp, pzn) to `out`.
            3. Inversion circuit: Inductor $L$ between pzp and n1, switch $S$ between n1 and pzn.
            Wait, if $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit. This flips the voltage of $C_p$ before the rectifier, allowing more charge to flow.
            Tuning $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.

    *   **Design 3: SSHI with a Zener Clamp**
        *   Topology: Same as Design 2, but add DZ33 on `out`.
        *   Rationale: SSHI increases power for S2/S4, and Zener prevents S3 overvoltage.

    *   FBR with Zener: Simple, handles S3 $V_{max}$, but might fail S2/S4 $V_{min}$.
    *   SSHI (inductor-switch flip) + Zener: Increases efficiency (helps S2/S4) and limits voltage (helps S3).

    *   Piezo: (pzp, pzn)
    *   L1: (pzp, n1)
    *   S1: (n1, pzn), ctrl: G1
    *   G1: SYNC, edges: "both", phase: 0.0, ton: (calculated later by the optimizer, but typically $\pi \sqrt{L C_p} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{5\text{mH} \times 25\text{nF}} \approx 35\text{ $\mu$s}$).
    *   Rectifier:
        *   D1: (pzp, out), DSCH
        *   D2: (pzn, out), DSCH (Wait, FBR needs 4 diodes)
        *   Actually, let's use a standard FBR:
            D1: (pzp, out), DSCH
            D2: (pzn, out), DSCH
            D3: (0, pzp), DSCH
            D4: (0, pzn), DSCH
    *   Storage: C1: (out, 0)
    *   Clamp: D5: (0, out), DZ33

    Wait, a full bridge rectifier (FBR) usually connects the AC source to a DC load.
    AC nodes: A, B. DC nodes: +, -.
    D1: A $\rightarrow$ +
    D2: B $\rightarrow$ +
    D3: - $\rightarrow$ A
    D4: - $\rightarrow$ B
    In this case:
    A = pzp, B = pzn, + = out, - = 0.
    D1: (pzp, out)
    D2: (pzn, out)
    D3: (0, pzp)
    D4: (0, pzn)

    Is this a valid SSHI?
    The inversion happens at the piezo terminals. The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo.
    Piezo (pzp, pzn)
    L: (pzp, n1)
    S: (n1, pzn)
    When S closes, $L$ and $C_p$ swap the charge. This happens at the voltage extrema.
    This should increase the amount of charge delivered to the rectifier per cycle.

    *   **Proposal 1: FBR + Zener (Baseline modification)**
        - Full bridge (4 DSCH)
        - C_out
        - DZ33 on `out`
        - Rationale: Basic overvoltage protection.

    *   **Proposal 2: SSHI + FBR (Power Boost)**
        - SSHI inversion circuit (L, S, SYNC)
        - Full bridge (4 DSCH)
        - C_out
        - Rationale: Higher power extraction to solve S2/S4 $V_{min}$.

    *   **Proposal 3: SSHI + FBR + Zener (Full Solution)**
        - SSHI inversion circuit (L, S, SYNC)
        - Full bridge (4 DSCH)
        - C_out
        - DZ33 on `out`
        - Rationale: Combines power boost and overvoltage protection.

    S1: Ip=50u, f=100, Cp=25n, RL=330k
    S2: Ip=50u, f=100, Cp=25n, RL=150k (Harder)
    S3: Ip=100u, f=100, Cp=25n, RL=2200k (Voltage too high)
    S4: Ip=30u, f=100, Cp=25n, RL=1000k (Weak)
    S5: Ip=40u, f=80, Cp=25n, RL=470k (Low freq)
    S6: Ip=50u, f=100, Cp=30n, RL=330k (Hot)

    SSHI is very effective at increasing the average harvested power. A Zener is essential because S3's light load (2.2M) and strong excitation will drive $V_{out}$ very high.

    *Self-Correction on SSHI Topology:*
    Is the inversion circuit L1:(pzp, n1), S1:(n1, pzn) correct?
    Yes, when S1 closes, the loop pzp-L1-n1-S1-pzn-Cp-pzp forms an LC resonant circuit.

    *Wait, what about the diode drops?*
    DSCH is ~0.25V. In an FBR, current passes through two diodes (one forward, one return). Total drop $\approx 0.5\text{V}$.
    $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$. $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$.
    If SSHI increases the effective $V_{oc}$ or just the charge transfer efficiency, $V_{out}$ will be higher.

    - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
    - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
    - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
    - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    - C1: out -> 0
    - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    - L1: pzp -> n1
    - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0.0)

    Let's refine the components:
    - D1: (pzp, out) DSCH
    - D2: (pzn, out) DSCH
    - D3: (0, pzp) DSCH
    - D4: (0, pzn) DSCH
    - D5: (0, out) DZ33
    - C1: (out, 0) 2.2uF (initial value, optimizer will tweak)
    - L1: (pzp, n1) 10mH (initial value, optimizer will tweak)
    - S1: (n1, pzn) ctrl G1
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0.0, ton: 30uS)

    This is 9 components. Well within the 16 component limit.

    Actually, I will provide three variations:
    1. `fbr_zener`: FBR + Zener.
    2. `sshi_fbr`: SSHI + FBR.
    3. `sshi_fbr_zener`: SSHI + FBR + Zener.

    Wait, let me double check if the `S` switch logic and `SYNC` work as intended.
    "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    Piezo current $I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    Zero crossings of $I_p$ are at $t = 0, \pi/\omega, \dots$
    At these times, the voltage $V_{Cp}$ is at its maximum/minimum.
    Closing the switch at the voltage extrema is exactly what SSHI requires to flip the voltage. Perfect.

    One more thing: the FBR.
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    If $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, D1 conducts. Current flow: pzp -> out.
    If $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$, D2 conducts. Current flow: pzn -> out.
    If $V_{pzp} < 0$, D3 conducts. Current flow: 0 -> pzp.
    If $V_{pzn} < 0$, D4 conducts. Current flow: 0 -> pzn.
    This is a standard full-bridge.

    Wait, the `S3` condition $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ is strict. The DZ33 Zener breaks down at 3.3V, so $V_{out}$ will be clamped around 3.3-3.4V. This should satisfy $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$.

    Let's review the `vavg` for S2. S2 has a heavy load (150k).
    The FBR alone failed ($V_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$). SSHI should boost this.

    Final check on component count for `sshi_fbr_zener`:
    4 diodes (FBR) + 1 diode (Zener) + 1 capacitor + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 SYNC = 8 components.

    Let's consider if there's any other topology. Maybe a half-bridge if the piezo were centered? But the piezo is between pzp and pzn. A full bridge is the most robust way to handle the AC.

    Is there any risk with SSHI? The $t_{on}$ needs to be precise. The optimizer will handle $t_{on}$ and $L$.

    Another option: a charge pump? No, too many components and complex.
    Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE)?
    SECE typically uses a switch to connect the piezo to the storage cap only at the peaks.
    But SSHI-L is generally more powerful.

    Wait, let's check the `SYNC` phase.
    "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation period (-0.25..0.25).
    For SSHI, we want the switch to close exactly at the peak.
    The peaks of $V_{pzp}$ (voltage) occur when $I_p$ (current) is zero.
    The `SYNC` triggers at the zero crossings of $I_p$.
    So `phase: 0.0` is correct.

    `fbr_zener`:
    - D1: pzp, out, DSCH
    - D2: pzn, out, DSCH
    - D3: 0, pzp, DSCH
    - D4: 0, pzn, DSCH
    - D5: 0, out, DZ33
    - C1: out, 0, 2.2uF

    `sshi_fbr`:
    - D1: pzp, out, DSCH
    - D2: pzn, out, DSCH
    - D3: 0, pzp, DSCH
    - D4: 0, pzn, DSCH
    - C1: out, 0, 2.2uF
    - L1: pzp, n1, 10mH
    - S1: n1, pzn, G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton=30uS, phase=0.0, edges=both

    `sshi_fbr_zener`:
    - D1: pzp, out, DSCH
    - D2: pzn, out, DSCH
    - D3: 0, pzp, DSCH
    - D4: 0, pzn, DSCH
    - D5: 0, out, DZ33
    - C1: out, 0, 2.2uF
    - L1: pzp, n1, 10mH
    - S1: n1, pzn, G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton=30uS, phase=0.0, edges=both

    Wait, the `S` switch is between `n1` and `pzn`, and `L` is between `pzp` and `n1`.
    So when `S1` is closed, the circuit is `pzp -> L1 -> n1 -> S1 -> pzn`.
    This is in parallel with the piezo `pzp-pzn`. Correct.

    One detail: "ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp)".
    If $L = 10\text{mH}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$:
    $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.14 \times 1.58 \times 10^{-5} \approx 49\text{ $\mu$s}$.
    The optimizer will find the best $t_{on}$ and $L$.

    Let's double check the Zener direction.
    "zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at 3.3 V)."
    So `nodes: ["0", "out"]` is correct for DZ33.

    Let's make sure we don't exceed 16 components.
    `sshi_fbr_zener` has 9 components (4 diodes, 1 Zener, 1 cap, 1 inductor, 1 switch, 1 SYNC). This is fine.

    Wait, for the `S` switch: `S` takes `nodes [a, b]` and `ctrl: id of a SYNC`.
    `G1` is the `id` of the `SYNC`.
    The components list for `SYNC` says: "no nodes".
    So I should list `G1` as a component with type `SYNC`.

    Let's write the JSON.
